title: Cinsiyetçi Teknik Direktör'e tepki
content:
Türkiye Futbol Federasyonu 1'nci liginde oynayan Muğlaspor'un geçtiğimiz günlerde basınla tanışma toplantısı vardı. Toplantıda Teknik Direktör Yalçın Koşukavak'ın kadın gazetecilere yönelik cinsiyetçi sözleri tepki topladı. Muğlaspor Teknik Direktörü Yalçın Koşukavak’ın kadın gazetecilere yönelik “Bilsem kısırımı da altınımı da alırdım, gün yapardık” ve “Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur” sözlerine kadın gazeteciler ve kadın örgütleri tepki gösterdi. Muğlaspor Kulübü ise sözlerin “espri amacı taşıdığını” ve bağlamından koparıldığını savundu.


Muğlaspor Teknik Direktörü Yalçın Koşukavak ile 20 Ağustos’ta Muğla’nın Akyaka Mahallesi’nde futbolcular, aileleri, teknik heyet ve basın mensuplarının katıldığı bir kahvaltı etkinliği düzenlendi. Toplantının başında kulüp başkanı ve yöneticiler mekandan ayrıldı. Koşukavak'ın basın toplantısı için hazırlık yapılırken gazetecilerin oturduğu masa teknik direktör için hazırlanmaya başladı. 


Kahvaltığı basın toplantısını 7 kadın ve 4 erkek muhabir takip ediyordu. Koşukavak, sözlerine "Daha önce basın toplantısında bu kadar bayan görmemiştim. Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur. Bilsem kısırımı da altınımı da alırdım, gün yapardık" diyerek başladı.


Etkinlikte yaşananları Mabolla Medya muhabiri Esma Turan; Koşukavak’ın sözlerini ise Bodrum Kadın Dayanışma Derneği’nden Figan Erozan ve Evrim İnan bianet’e değerlendirdi.


Turan: Bu sözleri 'espri' olarak değerlendirmiyorum


Mabolla Medya muhabiri Esma Turan, kahvaltı etkinliğinde bulunan kadın gazetecilerden biriydi. Etkinlik öncesi ve sırasında yaşananları anlatan Turan şöyle konuştu:


“Toplantı öncesinde kulüp başkanı, yöneticiler ve futbolcular ile kahvaltı yapıldı. Kahvaltı sonrasında sadece hocanın açıklama yapacağı söylendi. Aslında bir tanışma ve değerlendirme toplantısıydı. Yalçın Bey ile ilk basın toplantısı ve tanışma olacaktı. Kulüp başkanı ve yönetimi mekândan ayrıldı. Bizim masamız basın açıklaması için hazırlanıyordu. Biz mikrofonları hazırlarken hoca geldi, daha masaya oturmadan ve merhaba bile demeden kısır muhabbetini yaptı.”


Turan’ın aktardığına göre gazeteciler önce ne olduğunu anlamadı, ardından “Biz de gün yapmıyoruz burada” diyerek tepki gösterdi. Bunun üzerine Koşukavak, “Sizde soru da yoktur şimdi” dedi.


Turan, toplantıda yaşananları şöyle anlattı:


“Biz de kaldık, dinledik açıkçası. Ne yapacağımızı bilemedik yani kal geldi o sırada galiba. Sonradan keşke kalkıp gitseydik dedik. Sorularımız vardı, onları da sormadık. Erkek meslektaşlarımız da soru sormadı. Sadece Yalçın Bey konuştu. 7 kadın ve 4 erkekti gazeteciler.”


Tepkilerin toplantı sonrasında gazetecilerin kendi aralarındaki değerlendirmeleri ve konunun haberleştirilmesiyle ortaya çıktığını belirten Turan, “Haber yapmasalar olur mu? Kulübe zarar gelmesin, cumartesi maç var” denildiğini söyledi.


Koşukavak’ı kişisel olarak hedef almak veya Muğlaspor’a zarar vermek gibi bir amaçlarının olmadığını vurgulayan Turan şöyle devam etti:


“Muğlaspor, bu şehrin önemli bir değeri ve hepimiz kulübün başarılı olmasını istiyoruz. Biz orada söylenen sözleri duyduğumuz şekliyle, kayda geçtiği biçimiyle kamuoyuna aktardık.”


Muğlaspor Kulübü’nün olayın ardından yayımladığı açıklamaya katılmadığını belirten Turan, “Sizde şimdi soru da yoktur” ifadesini kadınların mesleki yeterliliğini ve gazetecilik mesleğini cinsiyet üzerinden değerlendiren bir yaklaşım olarak yorumladı.


Kadınları kamusal alandan dışlayan bir pratik


Bodrum Kadın Dayanışma Derneği de sosyal medya hesabından Koşukavak’ın sözlerine ilişkin bir açıklama yayımladı.


Açıklamada, “Bunu bir kişinin nezaketsizliği olarak değil, erkek egemen kurumların kadınları kamusal alandan dışlama pratiği olarak görüyoruz” denildi.


Koşukavak’ın “kısır” ve “altın günü” ifadelerine de tepki gösterilen açıklamada şöyle denildi:


“‘Kısır’ ve ‘altın günü’ üzerinden kurulan alay, kadınların dayanışma pratiklerini ve mesleki kimliklerini aynı anda küçümsemektedir.”


Muğla Barosu ve Menteşe Kadın Platformu: Münferit bir şaka değil


Menteşe Kadın Platformu ile Muğla Barosu Kadın Hakları ve Toplumsal Cinsiyet Eşitliği Komisyonu da Koşukavak’ın ifadelerine ilişkin ortak bir açıklama yayımladı.


Açıklamada Koşukavak’ın sözlerinin “münferit bir şaka” olmadığı belirtilerek şöyle denildi:


“Bu söylem; sporu, basını ve kamusal alanı yalnızca erkeklere ait gören, kadını ev içi rollerle, geleneksel kalıplarla ve edilgenlikle tanımlamaya çalışan ataerkil zihniyetin yansımasıdır.”

author: Unknown
title: Aslan: Local governments should institutionalize services in Kurdish
content:
Istanbul is not only Turkey’s largest metropolis but also one of the provinces where violence against women is particularly widespread. According to the 2025 report of the Association for Field Research, Istanbul ranks first in statistics on violence against women and femicides, at 6.4 percent. In addition, women whose first language is not Turkish generally lack access to services where they can seek help when they face attacks and abuse.


Istanbul, which has the largest Kurdish population among cities in Turkey, has no official institution providing services in the mother tongue. Kurdish is also not officially included in the work initiated by municipalities for women.


Derya Aslan, a board member of the Women’s Time Association, prepared the “Report on Monitoring Access in the Mother Tongue to Local Government Services for Combating Violence Against Women in Istanbul,” examining whether services in women’s native languages are provided in cases of violence against women in Istanbul. She spoke to our agency about women’s experiences and the findings of the report.


Violence against women is the result of the patriarchal system's domination


Aslan continued: “Assessing violence against women in Istanbul solely through individual incidents or femicides would be an incomplete definition of the reality. Violence against women is a result of the patriarchal system’s domination over women’s lives, bodies and will. In addition to physical, psychological, sexual and economic violence, excluding women from public life, rendering their labor invisible, impoverishing them and isolating them are also different manifestations of this system.


From the perspective of the women’s freedom struggle, we do not view violence merely as an issue between individuals. We believe that this system, which threatens women’s right to life, must be addressed together with its social, political and institutional dimensions. There is a system in which everything from femicides and impunity for violence to the exclusion of women from decision-making mechanisms and economic dependence reinforces one another.”


The existence of a service doesn't mean everyone can access it


Aslan said they had conducted a study on Kurdish women’s access to services in their mother tongue in Istanbul, and added: “The work we carried out as the Women’s Time Association starts precisely from this point. We conducted a field-based study monitoring Kurdish women’s access in their mother tongue to municipal services for combating violence against women in Istanbul. We spoke with all 39 district municipalities in Istanbul as well as Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, examining existing services, their capacity to provide services in Kurdish, and women’s access to these services. We turned the results of our fieldwork into a report, shared it with the public, and developed concrete policy recommendations for local governments.


In this respect, this is one of the first studies to monitor Kurdish women’s access to violence-prevention services in their mother tongue in Istanbul within this framework. For us, the fundamental issue here is this: The existence of a service does not mean that the service is accessible to everyone. If there are barriers preventing a woman from accessing a service because of her language, identity or social position, we cannot speak of equality. Therefore, we do not view the struggle merely as intervening after violence has occurred. Strengthening women’s organized power, transforming social awareness, and building a women’s freedom-oriented way of life are the fundamental pillars of the struggle against violence.”


Women can express themselves more powerfully in their mother tongue


Aslan underlined that Kurdish women’s inability to receive services in their mother tongue cannot be regarded merely as a communication problem. She added: “From our perspective, the mother tongue is not merely a means of communication; it carries identity, memory, culture and social existence. Therefore, a Kurdish woman’s inability to receive services in her own mother tongue cannot simply be regarded as a communication deficiency.


For a woman subjected to violence, expressing the trauma, fear and violence she has experienced is already extremely difficult. The language in which a woman can express herself most powerfully is her own mother tongue. When barriers are placed in the way of her speaking her own language, her right to speak and to be a …

author: Freedom Shop Aotearoa
title: bell hooks On Patriarchy
content:
This article is presented as two imposed PDFs intended to be printed on A4 paper, resulting in an A5 saddle-stitched pamphlet. The first PDF is a single-sided cover intended to be printed in colour, the second double-sided inside pages intended to be printed in black and white.

bell hooks (1952 – 2021) was born into a working class family in a small town in Kentucky. She published around 40 books ranging from childrens’ stories and cultural commentary to poetry and essays on race, class and gender, becoming known as one of the best US radical writers of recent times. This pamphlet compiles her classic essay Understanding Patriarchy and transcripts of three interviews from 1994, 2011 and 2015. In these interviews, hooks discusses the nature of the patriarchy, the growth of white supremacy in the US, the need for love, the role of humour, spirituality and intersectionality, and the difficuties of remaining relevant when immersed in the academic world. Hooks’ anger, warmth and humanity is evident in these interviews, and reading them makes you feel very annoyed that she’s dead, and you are never going to have the chance to talk to her in person. Given that, I’m afraid this is as good as it gets. Her writing is pretty damn cool, though.

author: Corey Larocque
title: No woman should face harassment from taxi drivers
content:
It’s tragic that Iqaluit women feel the need to consider alternatives to taxis out of fear for their safety but it’s great they’re standing up for themselves.


Next week, Rosalie DeMaio, a Nunavut Arctic College student, is hosting a community meeting so people can discuss how to develop alternatives so they don’t have to rely on taxis.


Women routinely face unwanted come-ons from drivers, she said in an

interview

 with a Nunatsiaq News reporter. (The news story about her concerns is on page 3 of this week’s paper).


DeMaio said a driver once called her “baby girl” when he asked about her night out at a bar. He offered her wine. She declined, saying she just wanted to go to bed.


He persisted.


“I said, ‘No, I want to go to bed.’ And he said, ‘You can go to my bed,'” DeMaio said, adding she has also been followed or watched after being dropped off.


The yuck factor of that story is off the charts.


No woman should be subjected to that kind of advance, but especially not while making use of what’s almost an essential public service.


It’s inappropriate, whether it’s when a woman is taking a taxi to the grocery store or home after going out for a drink with some friends.


Taxis are a vital part of how Iqalummiut get around. The service needs to be safe and reliable for everyone.


The number of people who attend DeMaio’s community meeting on Thursday at the YWCA-Agvik women’s shelter at 7:30 p.m. will be telling. It could give some indication how widespread this issue is.


Both the taxi company and the City of Iqaluit should take note of what’s going on and what people who attend the meeting have to say.


They should have more robust ways of rooting out offensive drivers.


Five years ago, the city’s recently revived public safety committee looked into the issue when taxi drivers were victims of some bored youths who

threw rocks

 at them.


Now, if some drivers are causing problems for Iqaluit women, maybe it’s an issue the

committee

 — which has been looking for

something to do

 — could tackle.


Some of the experiences DeMaio described happened when she took a cab home from a bar. It’s potentially dangerous if women are reluctant to take a taxi home after going out for drinks with a friend. They might choose to drive their own vehicle.


Caribou Cabs manager Rod Mugford said the company has not received a direct complaint from female passengers but has embarked on a human resources program aimed at avoiding problems by training drivers in safety, anti-harassment, sexual misconduct and cultural sensitivity.


Some of DeMaio’s remedies include a women-focused rideshare service, a Facebook group or carpooling app to reduce women’s reliance on taxis.


DeMaio has been looking around for funding to help develop a cellphone app that people could use to co-ordinate their own rideshares.


That should be a no-brainer. Some organization should come to her aid. How much can it cost to develop an app? Some Nunavut organizations have spent money on a lot more trivial things. Give her a little seed money and see if it makes a difference.


Because it’s terrible and unacceptable that women don’t feel safe riding with some taxi drivers.


DeMaio deserves credit for identifying a serious social issue, airing it out and for putting alternatives on the table. That’s how change starts.

author: Jasmine Mithani
title: She Defended Herself From Domestic Abuse. She’s on Trial for Murder Next Week.
content:
Keshia Golden’s advocates say the legal system is stacked against both Black women and survivors of domestic violence.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

Keshia Golden, a Black mother from the West Side of Chicago, turned down a plea deal months ago even though it put her at risk of at least 20 years in prison.

In October 2022, Golden was eight months pregnant and had just celebrated her baby shower. She says her boyfriend, Calvin Sidney, attacked her in the kitchen, slamming her head into the counter — her attorneys say that kind of violence was typical of their relationship, and resulted in dozens of police calls and multiple arrests. One of her public defenders said the fight moved into another room, and that’s when Golden defended herself. “I just wanted him to stop,” Golden told the Chicago Sun-Times, reflecting on the moment when she said she grabbed a kitchen knife and stabbed Sidney in the leg. The blade hit his femoral artery, and he died in a hospital. Golden was charged with first-degree murder shortly after.

Prosecutors offered her a chance to plead guilty to second-degree murder, also a felony, and avoid prison time by agreeing to probation for two years. But the cost was still too high.

With a felony on her record in Illinois, Golden would lose opportunities to get back on her feet as a survivor of domestic abuse. She would be ineligible for public housing, lose access to child care funds and be barred from working in health care, her chosen field. She wouldn’t be eligible for student loans to help her start another career. All this would hurt her ability to provide for her 3-year-old daughter, Ky’liyah, whose baby shower she had been celebrating.

Golden’s trial is scheduled to begin Monday, and as a Black woman charged with killing her abuser the odds are stacked against her. A plea deal would risk her livelihood, but a trial could result in her being separated from her child for decades. Organizers are rallying for prosecutors to drop all charges instead of what they see as a decision to punish a Black mother for trying to save her own life. The people demanding her freedom say if she had not acted, her life — and that of her daughter — would be on the line instead.

“What is a woman’s right to defend herself against her abuser? And why is her abuser entitled to harm her? Why have we normalized that?” asked Holly Krig, director of organizing at Moms United Against Violence and Incarceration, who has been advocating on Golden’s behalf.

Leigh Goodmark runs the Gender, Prison and Trauma Clinic at the University of Maryland’s law school, and specializes in supporting criminalized survivors. “What’s happening to Keisha is not all that different than what happens to many women who fight back against their abusive partners,” she told The 19th.

She said the charges and plea deal offered to Golden aren’t surprising. There are many factors stacked against survivors of domestic violence accused of murder.

Goodmark said survivors tend to tell the truth about what happened, thinking that authorities will understand the abuse they have suffered and that they acted in self-defense. But in reality, that just makes a defendant who easily confessed. Prosecutors typically only look at a single incident, not the holistic circumstances of prolonged abuse.

Sierra Bartlett’s job as a mitigation specialist is to learn about the history of clients being represented by public defenders in Cook County, which covers Chicago. When she interviewed Golden, it became clear that there had been too many prior incidents of domestic violence for her to coherently recall them all. Bartlett tracked down hospital records for Golden to get a better sense of the scope, and saw she was admitted to the emergency room when she was 18 weeks pregnant after being strangled. Strangulation can become deadly very quickly, but this wasn’t even one of the incidents Golden had remembered. It’s also a predictor of intimate partner homicide.

Three months before Sidney was killed, records viewed by The 19th show he was served a protective order mandating no contact with Golden. He allegedly punched her in the face; she was in her second trimester at the time.

The defense commissioned an outside domestic violence expert to weigh in on Golden’s experiences. Bartlett said the expert evaluated Golden over four separate meetings, and using the Danger Assessment, a tool widely used to …

author: Unknown
title: 8 kez uzaklaştırmaya rağmen bıçaklandı: Adana'da kadınlar Ayşe Katırcı için adalet istedi
content:
Adana’nın Yüreğir ilçesinde yaşayan 52 yaşındaki üç çocuk annesi Ayşe Katırcı, yaklaşık 10 yıl önce 25 yıllık evliliğini sonlandırdığı Arif Tanrıkulu’nun boşanmanın ardından da tehdit ve şiddetine maruz kaldı. Hakkında 8 kez uzaklaştırma kararı aldıran ve KADES üzerinden ihbarlarda bulunan Katırcı, eski eşinin kendisine kefen gönderdiğini, “sana mezarlık alacağım” diyerek tehdit ettiğini, silah ve bıçakla korkuttuğunu anlattı. Buna rağmen 9-10 Ağustos’ta Tanrıkulu, Katırcı’nın evine girerek onu 8 yerinden bıçaklayıp ağır yaraladı. Olayın ardından kaçan Tanrıkulu Pozantı’da yakalanarak 11 Ağustos’ta tutuklandı. Yoğun bakımda tedavi gören Katırcı ise hayati tehlikeyi atlattı. 17 Ağustos’ta hastanede konuşan Katırcı, eski eşinin serbest bırakılması halinde kendisini öldürmesinden korktuğunu belirterek en ağır cezanın verilmesini istedi.

Yaşanan saldırının ardından Adana Kadın Platformu, kentte artan erkek şiddeti ve kadın cinayetlerine dikkat çekmek amacıyla İnönü Parkı’nda basın açıklaması yaptı. Platform adına açıklamayı Seren Canbolat okudu.

Canbolat, Ayşe Katırcı’nın yaşadıklarının ülkedeki cezasızlık politikalarının somut örneklerinden biri olduğunu belirterek, kadınların yaşamlarını sürdürebilmek için verdikleri mücadeleye rağmen yeterince korunmadığını söyledi.

Canbolat, Katırcı hakkında daha önce alınan uzaklaştırma kararlarının neden etkin biçimde uygulanmadığını sordu. Tanrıkulu’nun Katırcı’yı tehdit etmesine rağmen bugüne kadar neden tutuklanmadığını da soran Canbolat, “Kadınların uzaklaştırma kararlarını neden etkin uygulamıyorsunuz?” diye sordu.

Kadın cinayetlerinin münferit olaylar olarak değerlendirilemeyeceğini belirten Canbolat, geçtiğimiz temmuz ayında bir hafta içerisinde üç kadının birlikte oldukları erkekler tarafından öldürüldüğünü söyledi.

Kadınların yaşam hakkının korunması yerine ataerkil aile yapısını güçlendiren politikaların gündeme getirilmesini eleştiren Canbolat, kadınların ve çocukların korunması, güçlendirilmesi ve toplumsal eşitsizliğin ortadan kaldırılması için kadın odaklı politikaların uygulanması gerektiğini ifade etti.

Canbolat, yetkililerin sorumluluğunun kadınların yaşamlarına ilişkin kararlar almak değil, onları şiddetten korumak olduğunu vurgulayarak, “Bu ülkede her gün en az üç kadın öldürülürken işiniz kadınların nasıl doğum yapacağı değil, işiniz cinayet mahalli ataerkil aileleri güçlendirmek hiç değil” dedi.

Açıklamanın sonunda 6284 sayılı Kanun’un etkin uygulanması çağrısı yapan Canbolat, “Göreviniz kadınları ve çocukları korumak, güçlendirmek ve eşitsizliği ortadan kaldıracak kadın odaklı politikalar yürütmektir. Göreviniz 6284 sayılı kanunu etkin uygulamak. Göreviniz uzaklaştırma kararlarını uygulamak” ifadelerini kullandı.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

From 11 to 14 August, Equality Now, together with


CLADEM Uruguay

 and


Proyecto Ikove

, carried out

advocacy, capacity-building and institutional coordination activities to drive reforms and improve the response to sexual violence in Uruguay

, as part of


the Regional Day of Solidarity with Victims and Survivors of Sexual Violence

, which is observed every 9 August.


Uruguay has taken significant steps to prevent and respond to gender-based violence. However, for many girls, adolescents and women who are survivors of sexual violence, accessing justice continues to involve overcoming legal, institutional and geographical barriers.


The numbers highlight the scale of the challenge: approximately


one in three people under the age of 18 has experienced some form of sexual violence

, and in


seven out of ten cases of sexual violence reported to the police, the victim is a child or adolescent

.


Against this backdrop, the new alliance between Equality Now and local organisations seeks to drive legislative and institutional change to improve access to justice for victims and survivors of sexual violence in Uruguay.


A roadmap to strengthen access to justice


The week began on 11 August at the Legislative Palace with the event

‘Barriers to access to justice in cases of sexual violence’

, which brought together national authorities, female legislators from different political parties, members of the judiciary, public prosecutors, civil society organisations and survivors.


During the opening session, the Vice-President of the Republic, Carolina Cosse, expressed Parliament’s commitment to continuing to drive this agenda forward: “You can count on Parliament to promote laws that enable better access to justice.”


At the event, together with our national partners, we presented


Strengthening Access to Justice for Survivors of Sexual Violence in Uruguay

, a document that analyses the extent to which international standards have been incorporated into the country’s legislation and institutions, identifies the main challenges and proposes recommendations to move towards a more effective state response, with a focus on human rights, gender and intersectionality.


The analysis acknowledges the significant regulatory and institutional progress made in Uruguay, but also identifies structural deficits and regulatory gaps that continue to limit effective access to justice for women, girls and adolescents who are survivors of sexual violence.


As


Sofía Quiroga

, Advocacy Officer at Equality Now, explained during the opening of the event, the challenge has two closely connected dimensions: improving the implementation of existing laws and continuing to align the legal framework with international human rights standards. In this sense, the document seeks to acknowledge the progress made in Uruguay, while also encouraging discussion around the challenges that remain, including the need to ensure timely, specialised justice that is free from stereotypes and discrimination for victims and survivors of sexual violence.


Consent must be at the centre


Currently, the Uruguayan Criminal Code does not define sexual offences on the basis of the absence of consent, but rather on the basis of the use of violence or threats, or of certain circumstances in which the law presumes violence. Uruguayan legislation has already taken significant steps by establishing that silence, a lack of resistance or the victim’s sexual history cannot be interpreted as indications of consent. However, lack of consent does not yet constitute the central element of criminal classification.


Gabriela Kletzel,

Senior Legal Advisor

at Equality Now, emphasised that incorporating consent as the cornerstone of the legislation would not mean introducing a paradigm entirely foreign to the Uruguayan legal system. On the contrary, it would allow for the deepening of transformations that have already begun in other areas of the law and bring them into line with international standards.

author: Yi Ling Pan
title: Queerness, neu zensiert
content:
Die Serie „The Untamed“ zählt zu den weltweit erfolgreichsten chinesischen Serien der letzten Jahre. Trotz Zensur bleibt die Liebe zwischen den beiden männlichen Protagonisten Wei Wuxian und Lan Wangji aus der „Boys Love“-Romanvorlage spürbar.

Vor sieben Jahren klickte meine Mutter beim Mittagessen erstaunlich schnell auf „Play“. Normalerweise muss sie immer kurz überlegen, wenn ich sie als Expertin für chinesische Popkultur nach neuen Serientipps frage. Diesmal war sie sich sicher, dass „陈情令“ („Chén Qíng Lìng”), „The Untamed”, unser neues Mahlzeiten-Entertainment werden sollte. Die Serie gehe in China gerade komplett durch die Decke, erzählte sie, vor allem wegen der Beziehung zwischen den beiden Protagonisten Wei Wuxian und Lan Wangji. In einer Xianxia-Welt zwischen Altem China und Fantasy, eleganten Kostümen, Martial Arts und Dämonen, streben beide als sogenannte Kultivierende nach spiritueller Vollkommenheit. Das ungleiche Duo freundet sich an und durchsteht zusammen jahrzehntelange Clan-Kämpfe.

In der beliebten Onlineroman-Vorlage „魔道祖师“ („Mó Dào Zǔ Shī”), „Grandmaster of Demonic Cultivation”, erklärte meine Mutter, sind die beiden ein Paar. Es war also explizit eine „Danmei“-Story. 耽美 („dān měi“), wörtlich übersetzt „sich der Schönheit hingeben“, bezeichnet Boys-Love-Geschichten aus China. In Japan als Genre entstanden und in Ostasien schon lange beliebt, inspirierte es zuletzt auch zunehmend westliche Produktionen, Stichwort „Heartstopper“ und „Heated Rivalry“.

Die Drehbuchautor*innen von „The Untamed“ jedoch mussten das Skript umschreiben. Denn zu dem Zeitpunkt war LGBTQ+-Content in China schon explizit verboten. Ende 2015 wurden Darstellungen von Homosexualität aus dem Fernsehen verbannt, 2017 auch aus dem Internet. So wurden aus Wei Wuxian undLan Wangji statt Liebhaber Seelenverwandte.

Neugierig geworden, schaute ich die erste Folge. Nach nicht einmal der Hälfte brach ich ab. Mir waren die Gesichter zu weiß und makellos, die Ästhetik zu glatt, erklärte ich meiner Mutter. Sie schaute allein weiter, leicht enttäuscht. Rückblickend war das nicht mein einziger Grund. Eine queere Story, in der Queerness zensiert wird: Das konnte ja nicht gutgehen, dachte ich mir.

Erst Jahre später schaue ich alle 50 Folgen. Und beginne, mich selbst zu hinterfragen. Ob nicht mein kritisches Urteil zu voreingenommen war von einer westlichen Sozialisation; einer dogmatischen Vorstellung von Queerness, für die diktatorische Mittel wie Zensur der Tod bedeuteten.

Ich grabe mich durch Fanforen, um den Erfolg der Serie besser zu verstehen. Schon 2021 knackte die Serie zehn Milliarden Views auf dem chinesischen Streamingdienst „Tencent TV“; auf „Douban“ hält sie ein Rating von 7,7, auf „IMDb“ 8,7, und ist mittlerweile auch auf „Netflix“ ein Hit. An Chi aus Peking erzählt mir auf dem chinesischen sozialen Medium „Rednote“, dass sie noch immer mit Fans aus ganz China an Drehorten wandern gehen und den Titelsong anstimmen, sobald sie sich sehen. Und: Fans weltweit feiern die Liebesgeschichte trotz der Zensur. Oder sogar gerade deswegen. Die Kanadierin Debbiesunfish schwärmt auf „Reddit“: „Wären es einfach nur zwei Männer, die intim miteinander werden, würde mich das nicht so sehr ansprechen wie die sehnsüchtigen Blicke, die stillen Momente, in denen im Hintergrund eine Flöte spielt, während die Kamera langsam wegschwenkt.“ Sie fügt hinzu: „Ich bin queer, und für mich ist es ein Genuss, queere Liebe auf diese für mich neue, ‚zensierte‘ Art zu erleben.“

Beim Schauen merke ich, wie ich selbst immer mehr in die Liebesgeschichte hineingesogen werde. Die Spannung zwischen beiden Männern ist von Anfang an angelegt, da sie absolut gegensätzlich scheinen: Wei Wuxian als sorgloser Regelbrecher, Lan Wangji hingegen als eine Art wandelndes Regelwerk, der, wenn er redet, meistens Wei Wuxian ermahnt. Dass Wei Wuxian schließlich den dämonischen statt des rechtschaffenen Pfades der Kultivierung wählt, dem hell gekleideten Lan Wangji fortan in Schwarz begegnet, vergrößert diese Spannung nur noch. Trotzdem wartet Lan Wangji sechzehn Jahre lang auf den gestorbenen Freund, was für viele Fans die Romantik der Serie ausmacht. author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Balik-Tanaw | When women rise, God’s mercy breaks in the boundaries
content:
By Klein Fausto Emperado Iglesia Filipina Independiente/Aglipay Central Theological Seminary

Isaiah 56:1, 6-7 Psalm 67:2-3, 5, 6, 8 Romans 11:13-15, 29-32 Matthew 15:21-28

The Canaanite woman came to Jesus carrying the suffering of her daughter. She cried, persisted, and refused to be silenced. Yet the disciples wanted her sent away. Her voice was treated as a disturbance. Her struggle was seen as someone else’s problem.

Women continue to face discrimination, violence, abuse, and the denial of their dignity. Patriarchy has become so deeply woven into our society and even our churches, that it is sometimes treated as normal. We silence women, question their leadership, and even deny their calling. Sometimes, women themselves become bearers of patriarchy and misogyny.

Yet the Canaanite woman would not leave.

Her persistence challenges a Church that is tempted to silence those who disturb our comfort. Her cry echoes in the voices of mothers, wives, and sisters of victims of the so-called drug war who continue to demand justice despite threats and harassment. It echoes in the courageous voice of an Aeta woman chieftain who stood before an inquiry on the proposed US-led Pax Silica, declaring that her people will not surrender their ancestral land, the land that sustains their life, culture, and future.

These are not merely voices of protest. They are voices of life.

The late Muriel Orevillo-Montenegro, a pioneer Asian theologian and author of “The Jesus of Asian Women” reminds us to encounter a Jesus understood through the lived struggles of the women of the Philippines and Asia, a Christ who accompanies people in their struggle against poverty, patriarchy, discrimination, and oppression, and who seeks life to flourish.

This is the Jesus we meet in the Canaanite woman’s struggle.

Isaiah declares that God’s house is for all peoples.

Psalm 67 proclaims God’s blessing among all nations.

Romans remind us that God’s mercy embraces all. The Gospel reveals that God’s mercy cannot be imprisoned

by boundaries created by human beings.

So where does the Church stand?

We cannot proclaim God’s inclusive mercy while silencing those who cry for justice.

We are called to journey with women, listen to the marginalized, amplify their voices,

defend their dignity, and stand with communities resisting oppression.

The Church must not become another instrument of empire, patriarchy, or exclusion.

When women rise and speak for healing and justice , the Church must listen. When the oppressed cry, the Church must stand. When people struggle for life, the Church must struggle with them.

This is the way of Christ: to serve the people, to seek justice,

and to make God’s liberating mercy visible in the world.

Let us join our voices in this prayer:

Pray with Me for a World of Mercy

Pray with me for a world where no one is turned away, where every table has room for the poor , and every person knows the abundance of God’s blessing.

Pray with me for the courage of the Canaanite woman, who would not be silenced, whose cry for mercy crossed every boundary and opened the way to healing.

Pray with me for those whose voices are drowned by power for women seeking justice, for Indigenous peoples defending their land, for the poor and oppressed whose dignity is denied.

Pray with me for a Church that listens, that welcomes, that stands with those at the margins, and refuses to send them away.

May our prayers become courage, our courage become solidarity, and our solidarity becomes action.

May God’s mercy reach every people, until justice flows freely and no one is left behind. Siya Nawa!

Balik-Tanaw is a group blog of Promotion of Church People’s Response. The Lectionary Gospel reflection is an invitation for meditation, contemplation, and action. As we nurture our faith by committing ourselves to journey with the people, we also wish to nourish the perspective coming from the point of view of hope and struggle of the people. It is our constant longing that even as crisis intensifies, the faithful will continue to strengthen their commitment to love God and our neighbor by being one with the people in their dreams and aspirations. The Title of the Lectionary Reflection would be Balik –Tanaw , isang PAGNINILAY . It is about looking back (balik) or revisiting the narratives and stories from the Biblical text and seeing, reading, and reflecting on these with the current context (tanaw).

title: and my take today is that framing misogynistic writing as an “inability to write female characters”…
content:
hierophagy

:

and my take today is that framing misogynistic writing as an “inability to write female characters” subconsciously takes away most of the blame, implying that women are an alien creature compared to men and that it is no fault of the writer because it’s out of their skill set. it’s not an inability, not a lack of expertise, it’s the simple refusal to consider women as individual people and give them the same depth and grace that comes easily to the writer when they write male characters. it’s not that christopher nolan, stephen king, james cameron (and frankly anyone using the argument, both professional and hobbyist; yes, that includes fanfic writers) etc can’t write women, it’s that they just won’t. at that point in time it is a conscious decision driven by the laziness to unpack their misogynistic biases, and should be addressed as such

author: anred
title: Once años de organización y lucha: llega el 11.º Encuentro Regional de Zona Sur
content:
El próximo 5 de septiembre, mujeres, lesbianas, travestis, trans, intersex, bisexuales y personas no binaries del conurbano sur se reunirán en Monte Grande para compartir experiencias, debatir las problemáticas de los territorios y fortalecer las redes de organización colectiva. La jornada tendrá talleres, feria autogestiva, caravana, rondas de debate y espacios de participación accesibles e inclusivos.

Por ANRed 


El próximo 5 de septiembre se realizará en Monte Grande el 11.º Encuentro Regional de Mujeres, Lesbianas, Travestis, Trans, Intersex, Bisexuales y No Binaries de Zona Sur, una nueva jornada de encuentro, organización y construcción colectiva que reunirá a quienes vienen sosteniendo redes y experiencias de lucha en los territorios del conurbano sur.


A once años de su primera edición, el encuentro vuelve a plantearse como un espacio para poner en común las problemáticas que atraviesan a los distintos territorios, compartir saberes y experiencias y construir herramientas colectivas frente a las desigualdades y las violencias. La propuesta recupera la memoria de los encuentros anteriores y busca, al mismo tiempo, fortalecer las redes comunitarias y proyectar nuevas formas de participación y organización.


“Como desde hace once años estamos aquí organizades para debatir, intercambiar pero sobretodo reafirmar nuestra lucha en este contexto adverso, crisis económica y ataque a nuestro transfeminismo que ha logrado cambios en la sociedad en estos últimos años. Les esperamos a todes quienes quieran participar de esta experiencia enriquecedora”, expresó una de las organizadoras.


Una jornada para encontrarse y organizarse


La jornada comenzará a las 10:30 en la Plaza de las Artes, donde será el punto de encuentro. A las 11:30 se realizará la apertura formal y comenzarán los talleres de autodefensa, primeros auxilios y violencia digital —Ley EMA—. Luego, a las 12:30, habrá una feria autogestiva para compartir producciones y seguir fortaleciendo los vínculos entre quienes participan.


A las 13:30 se realizará una caravana hacia el Instituto 35, donde continuarán las actividades con las rondas de debate. Desde las 14, los espacios de discusión abordarán distintas dimensiones de la vida cotidiana y las luchas territoriales: salud, cuidados y derecho a decidir; trabajo, precarización y derechos laborales; educación pública, acceso y organización; violencias, prevención y acompañamiento; y derechos humanos, memoria y defensa de las conquistas alcanzadas.


El cierre será a las 16, con una instancia de conclusiones destinada a recuperar lo trabajado durante la jornada y pensar colectivamente los próximos pasos.


Accesibilidad y participación


Uno de los ejes destacados de esta edición será la accesibilidad. El encuentro contará con un equipo de Lengua de Señas Argentina (LSA) para favorecer la participación de personas sordas y dispondrá también de un espacio de calma sensorial, pensado para quienes necesiten transitar la jornada con menor estímulo.


Desde la organización remarcan que la participación de todas las personas es fundamental para construir un encuentro verdaderamente inclusivo y proponen continuar derribando las barreras capacitistas que atraviesan los espacios y territorios.


En un contexto atravesado por la crisis económica y por disputas en torno a derechos y conquistas construidas durante años de organización, el encuentro se propone como un espacio para volver a encontrarse, intercambiar experiencias y reafirmar que la organización colectiva sigue siendo una herramienta fundamental.

author: Jeremy Kohler
title: Missouri GOP Attempts to Restore Abortion Ban With Anti-Trans Ballot Initiative
content:
Critics say the measure deploys misleading language while folding in restrictions on gender transition care for minors.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Two years ago, abortion opponents in Missouri tried to defeat Amendment 3, a ballot initiative to enshrine reproductive rights in the state constitution, by falsely telling voters that it would allow gender transition surgeries for minors — even though it wouldn’t.

Voters approved Amendment 3 anyway, overturning the near-total abortion ban enacted by Missouri’s GOP-dominated legislature that had taken effect after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade in 2022.

Now Republican leaders in the state are trying to repeal those rights again, using the same issue. They placed a new amendment on the November ballot, also called Amendment 3, that would restore Missouri’s abortion ban while allowing limited exceptions but also constitutionally prohibit gender transition care for minors — though the state has banned surgeries and new prescriptions of puberty blockers and hormones by law since August 2023.

For the Missouri GOP, Election Day can often seem like Groundhog Day. The party holds a supermajority in the legislature and controls every statewide office, yet voters have repeatedly used the initiative petition process to enact policies Republican leaders oppose. By gathering enough signatures, citizens have placed proposals directly on the ballot, then persuaded voters to expand Medicaid, legalize marijuana, raise the minimum wage and restore abortion rights.

This month, that disconnect became an electoral humiliation for Republican leaders. More than 80% of voters rejected their attempt to make it nearly impossible for citizens to amend the state constitution. It was even worse for Gov. Mike Kehoe’s plan to phase out the state income tax: More than 83% voted no.

Missouri Republicans have become “drunk with power,” said Ken Warren, a professor emeritus of political science at Saint Louis University and associate director of the SLU/YouGov Poll. “Because they control everything, they think they can do what they want — and they can’t.”

The new Amendment 3 on the November ballot shows how Republicans, using misleading language, a carefully chosen distraction and even a recycled name, are trying to undo one of those defeats. In 2024, a yes vote on Amendment 3 protected abortion rights. In November, voters will again be asked to vote yes on Amendment 3 — this time to take them away.

Republican leaders say voters never intended to approve a nearly unlimited right to abortion. They argue that Missourians would prefer an abortion ban with limited exceptions for rape, incest, medical emergencies and fetal anomalies — particularly when it is paired with restrictions on gender transition care for minors.

It would not take much to reverse the 2024 result. Abortion rights passed 51.6% to 48.4% — meaning a shift of about 48,000 voters would have defeated the measure.

Critics call the inclusion of gender care “ballot candy,” a way to make an unpopular proposal easier to swallow. They say the tactic is especially cynical because it promises voters a prohibition that, in large part, Missouri already has. State law already bans gender transition surgery for minors and, through August 2027, bars minors from starting puberty blockers or cross-sex hormones for gender transition. Amendment 3 would place the restrictions in the state constitution without an expiration date.

The two provisions bundled together differ enormously in scope. Repealing reproductive rights would affect the healthcare options available to a state with about 6.3 million people. The restrictions on gender transition care concern a small number of minors receiving highly specialized treatment.

Yet supporters want voters focused on the specter of children being used as lab guinea pigs, not the abortion rights the amendment would repeal. A new billboard in the St. Louis suburbs urges them to vote yes and “ban transgender surgeries for minors.”

A website for the political action committee behind the campaign, Her Health, Her Future — whose treasurer is Missouri first lady Claudia Kehoe — declares “OUR CHILDREN are not LAB EXPERIMENTS.” It says Amendment 3 would protect children from “harmful, sterilizing medical procedures” and restore “common sense health and safety standards” for women’s health clinics.

Neither message …

author: TGEU
title: The rise of binary laws and their impact on trans communities in Europe and Central Asia
content:
Across Europe and Central Asia, governments are increasingly introducing laws and policies that reinforce a strict gender binary, restricting the rights, healthcare and public lives of trans and gender diverse people.  


These developments are not isolated. Across very different political contexts, governments are adopting increasingly similar legal approaches, often justified through claims about protecting ‘children’, ‘women and families’, ‘national security’ and ‘traditional values’.


TGEU’s recent policy brief analyses this growing trend, asks how these policies are connected, and what they mean for trans communities and democracy more broadly.


get the policy brief


Why is this happening? 


The expansion of these policies is taking place alongside the growing influence of anti-gender, conservative and nationalist movements across the region. Political developments in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Russia have helped to strengthen these actors and contributed to the circulation of similar narratives and legal models across Europe and Central Asia.


Different countries, the same legal playbook


From Hungary and Bulgaria to Slovakia, Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Belarus and Türkiye, governments are introducing measures such as:


Defining sex strictly as male and female, based on biological characteristics


Eliminating or restricting legal gender recognition


Criminalising or banning trans-specific healthcare


Limiting rights related to family life, including marriage, parenting, and adoption


Introducing ‘anti-propaganda’ laws targeting gender diversity, sexuality, and bodily autonomy


Criminalising or restricting discussion of gender diversity


While the details differ between countries, the direction is increasingly similar: narrowing the space in law and society for people who do not fit a rigid gender binary.


For trans and gender diverse people, the consequences are exclusion from public life, forced disclosure of gender identity, greater risk of violence and shrinking spaces for trans communities. It also affects intersex people, families, and society by entrenching harmful legal and medical binaries.


get the policy brief


A warning sign for democracy


Binary laws are about more than technical legal issues. They are part of a wider process of democratic backsliding. Attacks on trans rights go hand in hand with restrictions on civic space, growing pressure on civil society, attacks on human rights defenders and efforts to weaken democratic participation and the rule of law.


This makes the rise of binary gender policies a concern not only for trans and gender diverse people, but for anyone working to protect human rights, democracy and open civic space.


Button: get the policy brief


TGEU’s position


TGEU calls on governments, institutions, and allies to:


Recognise binary gender laws as part of broader democratic backsliding


Respond early to the spread of exclusionary legal models


Ensure sustained, flexible funding for trans-led organisations


Defend legal gender recognition based on self-determination


Strengthen protection mechanisms for trans people and human rights defenders


The spread of binary gender policies is not inevitable. Understanding how these laws emerge, how they travel across borders and how they connect to wider attacks on democracy is essential to challenging them.


get the policy brief


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: Giovanna DeStefanis
title: Idaho Abortion Ban Blocked When Pregnancy Threatens Patient’s Health
content:
On August 13, 2026, a federal district court ruled in Idaho that the 14th Amendment protects the right to abortion when a pregnant person’s life or health is seriously threatened, blocking Idaho from enforcing its abortion bans in those circumstances.

The ruling invalidates two Idaho laws to the extent that they prohibit doctors from providing abortion care to patients facing serious medical conditions, including mental health conditions that put them at risk of suicide or overdose.

Following a six-day trial in June, the court determined that abortion care to prevent serious and lasting harm to a pregnant person’s health is deeply rooted in American history and tradition. The decision is the first federal court ruling since the overturning of Roe in 2022 to recognize that the federal Constitution continues to protect abortion access in certain circumstances.

The case was brought by the Lawyering Project and Legal Voice on behalf of Dr. Stacy Seyb, an Idaho maternal-fetal medicine specialist who argues that the state’s abortion bans prevented him from providing necessary care to patients.

The court’s ruling is particularly significant for patients experiencing serious mental health conditions. Idaho’s abortion bans previously prohibited abortion even when a pregnancy places a patient at risk of death from self-harm.

According to Idaho’s Maternal Mortality Review Committee, mental health conditions were the most common underlying cause of pregnancy-related death in the state between 2018 and 2024.

While this is a win, it’s important to note that the ruling does not establish a broader constitutional right to abortion. The court declined to block Idaho’s abortion bans when a fetus has a life-threatening condition unless the condition also poses a serious threat to the pregnant person’s health.

The decision comes as Idaho voters prepare to consider Proposition 1 or the “Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act Initiative” in November. This would establish a broader right to reproductive freedom, including access to abortion before fetal viability. Proposition 1 would go into effect on and after January 1, 2027.

This ruling is an important step toward protecting pregnant people from the devastating consequences of abortion bans. No one should be forced to carry a pregnancy that places their life or health in serious danger, and no doctor should face criminal punishment for providing medically necessary care. Pregnancy people must be able to make decisions about their own bodies and health without government interference.

If you are an Idaho resident, make sure you are registered to vote to make your voice heard on Proposition 1 this November!

author: By Niko Georgiades, Unicorn Riot
title: DJ-U: Creating a Network of Non-Binary People of Color
content:
Minneapolis, MN — Inside Wax World, Rosa Garcia’s South Minneapolis record store, the DJ known as Madre Rosa reflects on DJ-U, a program built from turntables, community, and care. After losing its funding, the free program that trained more than 100 non-binary artists of color may be coming to an end.


Unicorn Riot spoke with Garcia and DJ-U alum Makeda at Wax World about the program’s history, its impact and what could be lost if it ends. See our short

video special

 below with a

20-minute version

 underneath and shorts on

Garcia’s benefit-events

 and

messaging from visiting DJs

 further down in the article.


Piloted in 2016 at the queer underground space Madame of the Arts, and officially started in 2018, Garcia described DJ-U as a “reparations program” created to “repair that bridge that somewhere had gotten broken.”


DJ-U has been

outlined

 as a “skill-sharing/support community for Black/Indigenous women, queer, femme, and non-binary people of color.” The program’s mission is “to create a network of aspiring and experienced self-identified femme, non-binary people of color that have a shared passion for music and community.”


Through the program, artists are supported and empowered by mentors while being given access to DJ equipment, instructions, and connections to local venues and institutions “to ensure success and long term impact.”


With grant funding, DJ-U has been offered as a free program. The money from the grants goes straight to the DJs who are paid for teaching classes. Garcia said she’s “trying to continue to keep the dollars flowing in our community. If I’m going to get a grant, I want to help us build money, shared power, community, space.”


“We spread $100K pretty much during our ten years with this group of people,” said Garcia, “and it is meant to continue to generate in the DJ scene and rotate through this community.” She says that DJ-U has succeeded in changing the musical landscape of the Twin Cities with its DJ economy and promoting and connecting artists of color.


“There are hundreds of people every weekend that are hearing music that might have been touched by this program.”


Rosa Garcia (DJ Madre Rosa)


Recalling her experience eight years ago in DJ-U’s first program after its pilot, Makeda said the biggest gift from the program was being around “such cool and creative” people like fellow DJ-U alums

Yonci Jameson

 and

Dua Saleh

, and meeting “ambitious Black women and Black queer people my age.” “The ambition,” she says, is “the hardest thing to come by.”


She’s still connected to the mentors and other alum. “There’s been so many cool-ass people that I was able to share space with and learn from,” Makeda said. “It’s really nice to be surrounded with people that you want to be like, or you’re happy to be like.”


It’s not been an easy decade for DJ-U, however, as the program has borne the brunt of some traumatic tribulations in south Minneapolis over the last decade, including multiple building fires.


In 2018, DJ-U programming happened in a studio space with Garcia,

Ms. Lakesha

 and other artists in the Roberts Shoes building on Chicago Ave. and Lake St. before the building burned down — a

huge loss

 to the Minneapolis arts community. This forced the program to relocate.


In 2020, DJ-U was being held in a large 5,000 sq. foot room in the Ivy Building and then came the Coronavirus pandemic. In-person programming was suspended and just a few months later in late May, the building was set aflame from falling ashes during fires from the

George Floyd Uprising

.


This time their equipment wasn’t totaled but everything needed to be dried out after the sprinkler system in the building doused everything in the rooms.


In 2026, effectively their tenth year, DJ-U was impacted by the U.S. government’s deadly

Operation Metro Surge

 and has additionally lost its funding. However, Garcia said that “if folks would like to

donate to the program

, well maybe we could” have another year of programming.


On 36th Ave. and Lake St. in south Minneapolis, Garcia’s record store Wax World, was deeply impacted by the federal occupation. She was forced to close her store for three weeks.


Despite facing the hardships, Garcia still holds Open Decks, allowing for DJs to come in and DJ at her store and she still lends out and gives away equipment.


Additionally, in the realm of mutual aid, Wax World has held multiple benefit events, fundraising for local businesses that were …

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Trans killings prompt call for investigation, policy review
content:
Gabriela Women's Party Rep. Sarah Jane Elago together with representative from various LGBTQIA+ groups pose for a group photo after they filed a resolution at the House of Representatives on August 13, 2026. Photo from Gabriela Women's Party

“It is imperative that those responsible for these violent acts be held accountable to end the culture of impunity.”

The Makabayan bloc on August 13 filed House Resolution No. (HRN) 1369 urging the House Committee on Women and Gender Equality to conduct an investigation and review of existing policies after a series of trans killings from June to August.

The most recent case was the killing of Jang Caes Macawili, a trans woman who was shot multiple times at an internet cafe in Cebu City on August 10.

“[T]his pattern of violence, constitutes a severe violation of the right to life and security of person, and underscores the urgent need for legislative action to address hate crimes, strengthen protective mechanisms, and dismantle systemic discrimination that fuels such violence,” the resolution stated.

On June 20, trans woman Bella Lutap, 20, was found dead in an irrigation canal in Sitio Burnao, Zaragoza after being reported missing for three days.

The Nueva Ecija police identified her ex-boyfriend as the primary suspect. He was arrested and charged with murder.

Read: Justice sought for trans woman killed in Nueva Ecija

On July 15, Teddy Federico, a trans woman, indigenous youth leader, and a barangay agricultural worker was found dead eight days after being reported missing.

The investigation into her death is still ongoing. The Sangguniang Bayan Veruela adopted Resolution No. 346, urging the Philippine National Police (PNP) Veruela to expedite the investigation and submit a progress report to the council.

On July 28, Betty Benito, a trans woman from Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, was reported dead in a dense forest. She was found by the police and community members. The primary suspect in her killing has been arrested.

The resolution took note of the spate of trans killings in recent years, including the cases of Shalani Dolina, Kierra Apostol, Ren Tampus, Ali Macalintal, and Ebeng Mayor. It also reiterated the 2025 statement of the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) that flagged the spate of trans killings as “transfemicide”— gender-based killing driven by transphobia, misogyny, or systemic hatred.

Read: Recent killings of trans women prompt groups to push for LGBTQIA protection

“It is imperative that those responsible for these violent acts be held accountable to end the culture of impunity surrounding violence against marginalized communities,” the CHR statement read.

It urged the legislators and the administration for the passage of the Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity, Gender Expression, or Sex Characteristics (SOGIESC) Equality Bill and the Comprehensive Anti-Discrimination Bill (CADB). It also demanded proper investigation from the law enforcement agencies.

Bulatlat asked the Philippine National Police (PNP) for the 10-year data of victims of homicide and murder, stratified by gender identity, including transgender people. The agency has yet to respond to the request.

Gender rights groups ASEAN SOGIE Caucus, STRAP, Bahaghari, Pioneer Filipino Trans Men Movement, Transmasculine Philippines, and Relentlessly Chase welcome the filing of the resolution. “We hope this process will provide space for meaningful dialogue, evidence-based discussion, and the perspectives of transgender communities, families of victims, civil society organizations, and other stakeholders,” the groups said.

They stressed that for the resolution to have meaningful impact, investigation must proceed promptly and transparently while involving the transgender communities and victims families to legislative, policy, and institutional change.

The SOGIESC Equality Bill and CADB are proposed legislative measures that seek to prohibit and penalize systemic discrimination against marginalized groups, including transgender individuals.

“Every life lost proves how this violence extends beyond the individual. Behind every case is a loved one being mourned, a family desperately seeking justice, and a community simultaneously living in fear under a system that fails to protect its constituents,” the groups said. (AMU, DAA)

author: Nahuel Lag
title: Dolavon Produce: una experiencia agroecológica en el Valle Inferior de Chubut
content:
Por Mauricio Amaya


En Dolavon, las heladas marcan el calendario de quienes trabajan la tierra y cada cultivo requiere paciencia. Mientras buena parte del Valle Inferior del Río Chubut espera la llegada de la primavera, Rosa Ranguileo recorre el invernáculo donde cultiva verduras junto a su hijo. Allí, entre hileras de lechuga, espinaca, rúcula, acelga y hierbas aromáticas, sostienen un proyecto que hace apenas unos años parecía impensado: producir alimentos agroecológicos para la comunidad.


Hace tres años, una convocatoria de la Municipalidad de Dolavon cambiaba la rutina de un grupo de familias de esta localidad del departamento de Gaiman. Hasta ese momento,

Rosa Ranguileo apenas hacía plantines con su hijo en su casa y tenían una huerta en el patio; de repente pasaba a tener un campo para cultivar.

"En verano se vende mucho más porque también sembramos mucho más. Además del invernáculo, tenemos dos parcelas", cuenta Rosa, que es parte del

 proyecto Dolavon Produce

 o el Nodo Productivo, como lo llaman en este pueblo de casi 4.000 habitantes.  


“Comer sano cambió nuestra alimentación y la de la comunidad. Ese sabor de las verduras es inigualable y además sabemos que lo producimos con nuestras propias manos. Y la gente ve nuestro trabajo”, sintetiza. 

 El proyecto tomó forma en 2023 como parte del

Programa de Infraestructura para Entramados Productivos Regionales,

 articulado por el Ministerio de Obras Públicas de la Nación. El de Dolavon es uno de los 12 nodos que se proyectaron en todo el país. Un año después, con la llegada de Javier Milei a la Casa Rosada, la iniciativa se desfinanció y la responsabilidad quedó enteramente en manos del municipio, que recibió el apoyo de la Federación de Asociación Mutualistas de Chubut (FAMUCH) para sostenerlo. 


Foto: Dolavón Produce / Nodo Productivo


De recuperar la tierra a construir comunidad 


El ingeniero agrónomo Luis Ñancucheo es uno de los pilares de Dolavon Produce.

 Las dos hectáreas y media donde funciona el Nodo eran terrenos municipales degradados, que no tenían antecedentes productivos. Recuperarlas fue uno de los primeros desafíos.

"Con prácticas agronómicas relativamente simples, incorporando mucho abono y materia orgánica, logramos recuperar esos suelos y ponerlos a producir con muy buenos resultados", explica Luis. 


El objetivo inicial era sencillo en su formulación, aunque ambicioso en la práctica: que familias de la localidad pudieran

producir alimentos sanos para autoconsumo y comercializar el excedente, generando un ingreso sin que el acceso a la tierra fuera una barrera

. "Empezamos con nueve familias. A cada una se le asignó una parcela y al año siguiente ya habíamos ampliado el predio. Hoy son 32 familias las que forman parte del Nodo", precisa Luis.


También instalaron un sistema de riego por goteo para optimizar el uso del agua, una decisión clave en una región donde cada recurso debe administrarse cuidadosamente y donde el riego tradicional habría dificultado la producción. Para Ñancucheo, el mayor logro del proyecto fue más allá del trabajo sobre la tierra o de la comercialización de los productos. Las familias productores recibeb cada sábado a los vecinos para realizar venta directa de la cosecha en el Nodo y coordinan visitas y pedidos vía WhatsApp.


Foto: Dolavón Produce / Nodo Productivo


"Lo productivo en estos proyectos no suele ser un problema sino las relaciones entre las personas. Y ahí fue donde el proyecto resultó altamente exitoso." Al tiempo que sus trabajadores fueron aprendiendo y mejorando las tierras, el Nodo logró un sentido de pertenencia para las familias y empezaron a tejerse redes de apoyo en torno a la producción de alimentos. 


En ese sentido, Luis marca cómo el deterioro del poder adquisitivo durante los últimos años y la necesidad de multiplicar los medios para sostener cada economía familiar resultó un obstáculo para el desarrollo del Nodo durante el 2024 y 2025.  “Algunos de los productores debían salir a hacer una changa para completar sus ingresos y no podían atender su parcela —grafica Luis y agrega—. Pero creo que en esta crisis se fortalecieron esos lazos. El gran desafío fue acompañar a cada familia, entender qué le estaba pasando y ser solidarios."


Aunque hasta el momento ninguna de las familias productoras vive exclusivamente del trabajo en el Nodo, todas aún requieren de tener otro empleo para solventarse, la dimensión colectiva resulta fundamental y despertó interés en otros …

title: Se realizó el 22° Mathapi Apthapi Tinku, hostigado por las restricciones de Ciudad
content:
El histórico encuentro cultural indígena sufrió una repentina medida del Gobierno de la Ciudad, que le redujo a un único día la autorización para realizar el evento en el Parque Los Andes, donde se realiza hace largos años. La notificación llegó poco antes que comenzara el evento. Racismo institucional disfrazado de medida administrativa.

El 22° Mathapi Apthapi Tinku en Parque Los Andes el sábado 15 de agosto. Fotos: Nicolas Solo ((i))


Pocas horas antes del comienzo de la 22° edición del Mathapi Apthapi Tinku, el Gobierno porteño notificó que sólo autorizaba de manera parcial la realización del histórico encuentro cultural que reúne a comunidades y organizaciones indígenas. “Queremos denunciar la ruptura de un acuerdo”, señaló María Pomacusi Urquizu, integrante del pueblo quechua y del comité organizador del Mathapi Apthapi Tinku, en declaraciones a Negrx, medio de la comunidad afroargentina.


Desde hace 21 años, el encuentro se desarrolla durante tres jornadas: una primera jornada dedicada a la ceremonia y otras dos destinadas a la presentación de bandas y expresiones musicales de los pueblos originarios. Esta vez, tuvieron que trasladar la segunda jornada a la Mutual Sentimiento, a unas cuadras del parque.


“Esto es una medida que el Gobierno de la Ciudad está desarrollando con todos los espacios públicos, pero acá hay un plus que es el racismo”, afirmó Pomacusi Urquizu. Y agregó que la decisión atenta directamente contra pueblos indígenas que vienen trabajando para recuperar y fortalecer su identidad.


La elección del Parque de los Andes como espacio del encuentro no es casual. Se trata de un espacio atravesado por una fuerte carga histórica para las comunidades indígenas: allí descansó el Primer Malón de la Paz durante su paso por Buenos Aires. Para la organización, esa memoria convierte al parque en un territorio emblemático para la celebración y la reivindicación de los pueblos originarios.

La organización había iniciado las gestiones ante el Gobierno porteño el 2 de julio. Según relata Pomacusi Urquizu, decidieron canalizar el pedido directamente con Agustín Conti, presidente de la Comuna 15, luego de un intercambio ocurrido el año pasado en torno a la organización del evento.


El Mathapi fue declarado de interés cultural por la Legislatura porteña y, en 2025, también por la propia Comuna 15. La Universidad Nacional de las Artes reconoció institucionalmente el aporte de esta expresión de cultura viva y milenaria, mientras que el Instituto Nacional de la Música (INAMU) también declaró de interés cultural al encuentro.


“Con todos estos argumentos presentados y explicados, en un primer momento nos dijeron que sí, que no había problema, que avanzáramos con eventos y permisos”, contó la integrante del comité organizador.


La situación cambió el miércoles 12 a última hora, cuando la organización recibió la noticia de que la autorización no sería otorgada para las tres jornadas porque la Comuna había decidido unilateralmente reducir el encuentro a un solo día.


Entre los argumentos esgrimidos para limitar la actividad aparece la posibilidad de lluvias y el supuesto cuidado del césped del parque. Para la organización, ninguna de esas razones justifica impedir la realización de las jornadas restantes.


El Mathapi, explicaron, no es solamente un festival musical. Es un espacio de encuentro, transmisión y reproducción de saberes. Allí funcionan espacios de formación y actividades vinculadas con las infancias, entre ellas un espacio de guaguas. Durante más de dos décadas, el encuentro se construyó como una experiencia autogestiva y colectiva, sostenida por las propias comunidades y organizaciones que participan.


Por eso, limitar las jornadas no implica únicamente modificar un cronograma. Para sus organizadores, pone en cuestión las condiciones materiales que permiten que una práctica cultural indígena continúe creciendo y transmitiéndose …

title: Çiğdem Kılıçgün Uçar: Öcalan’s involvement in the resolution process is a guarantee for democracy
content:
The Urfa Provincial Organization of the Democratic Regions Party (DBP) held its 2nd Ordinary Congress under the slogan “Towards a Democratic Society with Free Leader.”


Speaking at the congress on Sunday, DBP Co-Chair Çiğdem Kılıçgün Uçar said the following:


“Commemorations are currently being held for those who lost their lives in the struggle for freedom in Kurdistan and Turkey. What matters is remembering those heroes. I commemorate our comrades with respect and gratitude. Turkey is going through a major test. After 100 years of denying the Kurds, it has reached a point where it now recognizes them as an interlocutor. Everyone must take the February 27 call (made by Öcalan in 2025) upon themselves. Mr. Öcalan has always insisted on peace. The patience of the Kurdish sons and daughters we have lost has brought us to this point. If Kurds had been recognized in this country’s laws, they would not have ended up in prisons. If the Kurdish people had been included in this country’s legal framework, no one would have had to endure such a devastating war.


Now there is a debate over the framework law. Yes, there are shortcomings, but Leader Öcalan says that ‘a door to the law is opening.’ It paves the way for our families to be reunited with their children. It also opens the way for the militants in the mountains, who have brought this political struggle to where it is today, to return and engage in politics. It is time to end the period of conflict and transition to democratic politics.


Some claim that we have “joined forces with the AKP.” This is a grave injustice. We wish the opposition forces had come together so that we could have engaged with them as our interlocutors. The path opened by Leader Öcalan should become a path for all of us. We have built all our institutional structures in response to the demands of the people.


Since the Constitution of 1921, Kurds have not been included in any constitution, but today those in power have been forced to give Kurds a place in the law. Kurds who were not recognized in Syria now have to be recognized. Kurds who have been denied in Iran are today choosing a third way. This offers the basis for a new path. And this, of course, has been made possible through the efforts of those we have lost.


We must stand united against special warfare policies. The Kurdish people have been through extremely difficult times. Just yesterday, for example, a Kurdish family was subjected to a racist attack in Zonguldak. This is, of course, a consequence of the climate of hatred that has been created.


The Commission on Disarmament and Politicisation will convene tomorrow. This commission will make important decisions. Leader Öcalan’s involvement in the resolution of the Kurdish question is a guarantee for democracy. All the policies that have been pursued to date must come to an end.


Debates over who will become president aside, we are going through a historic period. This process being conducted with the state will determine its approach toward the Kurds. It is a process that will determine how democracy is to be established. We will monitor and support the framework law, and we will intensify our struggle to ensure that it achieves its goal.”

author: Ash Sarkar
title: Racism Pushed Jason Arday to the Top of the News Agenda
content:
On Friday 14 August 2026, Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London. For three weeks, he had been at the centre of a campaign of public shaming that had turned every aspect of his life upside down. He is survived by his two children.


The sequence of events is important. Not long after Arday took up the post as chair of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023,

David Harris

 (an emeritus professor at Plymouth Marjon University, whose work has been sceptical of critical race theory) contacted the university along with Martyn Hammersley, a sociologist at the Open University, about what they viewed as similarities between a paper of Arday’s from 2018, and an earlier paper led by epidemiologist Anjum Memon. A few months later, two of Arday’s papers were appended with corrections post-publication.


In September 2025, Jack Grove, a reporter at Times Higher Education (THE), was investigating claims that Arday had plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis. He contacted Arday for right of reply, and submitted a dossier of evidence to both Cambridge and the awarding university, Liverpool John Moores. THE was preparing to publish a story on the allegations. THE dropped the story after receiving a legal letter sent by notorious libel firm Carter-Ruck; in February of this year, Grove was

warned by police

 not to contact Arday again, having received a complaint of harassment.


Liverpool John Moores conducted an inquiry into academic misconduct, and characterised citation problems in Arday’s work as “

honest and reasonable error

”. 


After the THE investigation stalled,

Nathan Cofnas

 – a self-described “race realist” argued that black people “would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sport and entertainment” under a meritocratic system and who was fired by his Cambridge college in 2024 – began investigating the claims against Arday after being contacted by a member of the Cambridge faculty. He wrote about Arday on his Substack, claiming he had put Arday’s work

through plagiarism detection software

. With Cofnas’ post gaining traction, the plagiarism allegations began to break into the mainstream press.


Though the initial coverage of Arday was about alleged plagiarism in academic papers, soon reporters were pulling apart his entire biography. Articles were published disputing claims he had held visiting professorships, completed a master’s at Birkbeck, published a book with Palgrave Macmillan, raised millions for charity, and undertaken extraordinary feats of endurance running.


His forthcoming autobiography,

Great and Unfortunate Things

, was another object of investigation. The Times obtained an earlier 45-page proposal containing still more extraordinary episodes (a teenage car crash left him in a coma with locked-in syndrome, that doctors wanted to withdraw life support, and that he later survived testicular cancer) which did not appear in the finished memoir. Arday resigned from Cambridge on 5 August.


Between 24 July 2026, when the plagiarism allegations were first reported by The Telegraph, and 14 August 2026, when his death was reported, the British press published

249 articles about Arday

 – most of them

after

 he had resigned from his post. The instances of alleged fabrication were expansive, and raised serious questions about whether Arday’s memoir had been properly fact-checked. But inside the raging whirlwind of articles and accusations, a man’s life was being torn apart.


“I have a family,” wrote Arday in his

resignation statement

. “I want to be present for them.” The pressure had taken him to “the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.” 


Where is the line drawn between investigative rigour and a media onslaught? Nobody who finds themselves the subject of interrogative reporting experiences it as dispassionate, neutral scrutiny. They’re having their entire world upended, their flaws and their frailties exposed for the world to see. Fundamentally, journalism is a dynamic of predator and prey, in service of the public interest. But public interest is just one consideration; there is also proportion, and due prominence, that need to be kept in mind. 


There were legitimate questions to be answered by Arday, about his research and his account of his life. But it should never have been a front-page story. Even if all the worst things that were said about him turned out to be true, he was not the biggest nor most pressing issue …
